Ask about Luigi Ferrucci's research

Answers are drawn only from Luigi Ferrucci's published papers listed on this page, with each point linked to its paper. They describe what the papers report, not personal views or advice from Luigi Ferrucci. This is not medical advice.

Try

Longitudinal epidemiology of human aging, physical function, chronic inflammation, and biomarkers of biological age.

  • Lower-extremity function. Co-developed the Short Physical Performance Battery, which predicted disability, nursing home admission and mortality, and showed in pooled cohorts that gait speed is associated with survival (JAMA 2011).
  • Inflammation and aging. Showed that elevated interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein predict mortality in older adults, and reviewed chronic low-grade inflammation in ageing, cardiovascular disease and frailty.
  • Sarcopenia and muscle. Contributed to the FNIH project defining criteria for weakness and low lean mass, and linked skeletal muscle mitochondrial energetics to walking speed in older adults.
  • Biological age. Co-author of the DNAm PhenoAge and GrimAge epigenetic clocks, and characterized a plasma proteomic signature of age in healthy adults.

  1. 1
    12% lowerrisk of death for every 0.1 m/s faster walking speed

    Across nine cohort studies of older adults, faster usual walking speed went with longer survival over the full range of speeds. At age 75, predicted 10-year survival ranged from 19% to 87% in men and from 35% to 91% in women depending on walking speed, and age, sex and walking speed together predicted survival as well as models using chronic diseases, blood pressure and hospital stays.

    Studenski et al. 2011 · JAMAPooled analysis of 9 cohorts, 34,485 adults aged 65+ followed 6 to 21 years
  2. 2
    4.2-4.9xhigher risk of disability four years later with the lowest physical performance scores

    Among people over 70 who reported no disability, those who scored lowest on a short test of balance, walking speed and rising from a chair were 4.2 to 4.9 times as likely to be disabled four years later as those who scored highest. Intermediate scores carried 1.6 to 1.8 times the risk.

    Guralnik et al. 1995 · N Engl J MedProspective cohort of 1,122 non-disabled adults aged 71+ followed for 4 years
  3. 3
    3 simple testsbalance, an 8-foot walk and five chair stands predict disability, nursing home admission and death

    A short battery of physical performance tests (now known as the Short Physical Performance Battery) was strongly linked to self-reported disability and predicted death and nursing home admission. Even among people reporting almost no disability, scores separated a clear gradient of risk.

    Guralnik et al. 1994 · J GerontolPopulation study of more than 5,000 adults aged 71+ in three US communities
  4. 4
    2.6xhigher risk of death with high interleukin-6 and high C-reactive protein together

    In healthy, non-disabled older people, those in the top quarter of interleukin-6 had about twice the risk of death over 4.6 years, and those with both interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein elevated were 2.6 times as likely to die. The link held for heart and non-heart deaths and after adjusting for other risk factors.

    Harris et al. 1999 · Am J MedProspective cohort of 1,293 non-disabled older adults (Iowa 65+ Rural Health Study)
  5. 5
    1.76xhigher risk of mobility disability with the highest interleukin-6 levels

    Older people without disability who had the highest blood levels of interleukin-6 were 1.76 times as likely to develop mobility disability over four years. Risk rose quickly once levels passed about 2.5 pg/mL.

    Ferrucci et al. 1999 · J Am Geriatr SocNested case-control study of 633 adults aged 71+ followed for 4 years
  6. 6
    Muscle strengthexplains much of why high interleukin-6 speeds up physical decline

    Older women with the highest interleukin-6 levels had a 1.5 times higher risk of mobility disability and faster declines in walking speed. Accounting for their faster loss of knee strength weakened this link, pointing to muscle loss as one path from inflammation to disability.

    Ferrucci et al. 2002 · J Am Geriatr SocCohort of 620 older women with disability followed over 3 years (Women's Health and Aging Study)
  7. 7
    Partly explainedrise in inflammation with age by heart disease and its risk factors

    Interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, fibrinogen and other inflammatory markers were higher in older people. Adjusting for cardiovascular risk factors and disease made much of the age effect smaller, so part of the "pro-inflammatory state" of old age comes from these conditions.

    Ferrucci et al. 2005 · BloodPopulation study of 1,343 people aged 20 to 102 (InCHIANTI)
  8. 8
    PhenoAgea DNA methylation clock that predicts death, cancer, physical function and Alzheimer's disease

    Training a blood DNA methylation measure on a clinical measure of biological age, rather than on calendar age, produced DNAm PhenoAge. It predicted death, cancers, healthspan, physical function and Alzheimer's disease better than earlier clocks, and faster PhenoAge went with more activity in inflammation and interferon pathways.

    Levine et al. 2018 · Aging (Albany NY)Development and validation in multiple large cohorts with blood DNA methylation data
  9. 9
    GrimAgethe DNA methylation clock that best predicted time to death

    DNAm GrimAge combines methylation-based estimates of seven blood proteins and smoking pack-years. It outperformed other epigenetic clocks for predicting time to death, heart disease and cancer, and was linked to fatty liver, number of chronic conditions and age at menopause.

    Lu et al. 2019 · Aging (Albany NY)Development and validation in thousands of people from several cohorts
  10. 10
    76 proteinsform a blood signature of age that predicts chronic disease and death

    Of 1,301 plasma proteins measured in people aged 21 to 102, 651 changed with age, many tied to inflammation, the extracellular matrix and senescent cells. A 76-protein signature of age predicted the build-up of chronic diseases and death from any cause.

    Tanaka et al. 2020 · ElifePlasma proteomics in 997 adults aged 21 to 102
  11. 11
    GDF15the blood protein most strongly tied to age in healthy people

    In 240 healthy adults free of disease, 217 of 1,301 plasma proteins were linked to age, and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) had the strongest link. A 76-protein model tracked calendar age closely (r = 0.94).

    Tanaka et al. 2018 · Aging CellPlasma proteomics in 240 healthy adults aged 22 to 93
  12. 12
    Faster agingmeasured over years predicts decline, disease and death better than one-time measures

    Combining how far each person drifts from typical trajectories in body composition, energy use, internal balance and brain health, measured repeatedly over time, gave a longitudinal measure of aging. Faster aging on this measure went with faster physical and cognitive decline, more chronic disease and shorter survival, more robustly than single-time-point clinical or epigenetic measures.

    Kuo et al. 2022 · Nat AgingLongitudinal phenotyping across adulthood in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging
  13. 13
    4.9xhigher risk of dementia with severe hearing loss

    Over about 12 years, dementia risk rose steadily with worse hearing, by 27% for every 10 decibels of loss. Compared with normal hearing, risk was 1.9 times higher with mild, 3.0 times with moderate and 4.9 times with severe hearing loss.

    Lin et al. 2011 · Arch NeurolProspective cohort of 639 dementia-free adults (Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging)
  14. 14
    41% fasterdecline in global thinking scores in older adults with hearing loss

    Older adults with hearing loss had 41% and 32% faster yearly declines on two thinking tests than those with normal hearing, and a 24% higher risk of developing cognitive impairment over six years. Decline was steeper the worse the hearing loss.

    Lin et al. 2013 · JAMA Intern MedProspective cohort of 1,984 adults with mean age 77 followed for 6 years (Health ABC)
  15. 15
    6.3xhigher risk of dementia when memory and walking speed decline together

    Compared with people aging typically, those whose memory declined had 3.5 times, and those whose walking slowed had 2.2 times, the risk of dementia. People with both declines had 6.3 times the risk.

    Tian et al. 2020 · JAMA Netw OpenIndividual-level meta-analysis of 6 cohorts, 8,699 adults aged 60+
  16. 16
    Less sleeplinked to more amyloid in the brain

    In older adults from the community, reports of shorter sleep and poorer sleep quality went with more beta-amyloid, the protein that builds up in Alzheimer's disease, on brain PET scans.

    Spira et al. 2013 · JAMA NeurolCross-sectional PET study of 70 adults with mean age 76 (Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging)
  17. 17
    89.6%accuracy of blood vesicle markers in predicting Alzheimer's disease years before symptoms

    Brain-derived vesicles in blood from people who later developed Alzheimer's disease carried more phosphorylated tau and altered insulin signaling proteins than in matched controls, years before symptoms. A model built on these markers reached an area under the curve of 89.6% and 80% when tested in a separate set.

    Kapogiannis et al. 2019 · JAMA NeurolCase-control study of 887 plasma samples from 350 people (Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging)
  18. 18
    <26 kg / <16 kggrip strength cut-offs for weakness in older men and women

    Pooling nine studies, the FNIH Sarcopenia Project recommended defining weakness as grip strength under 26 kg in men and 16 kg in women, and low lean mass as arm and leg lean mass adjusted for body mass index under 0.789 in men and 0.512 in women.

    Studenski et al. 2014 · J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med SciPooled analysis of 26,625 older adults from 9 study sources
  19. 19
    Frailtyconfirmed as a distinct syndrome that predicts disability and death

    A standard definition of frailty (weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slowness and low activity) behaved as a single syndrome in older women. Women classified as frail were more likely to become disabled, enter long-term care and die, independently of other factors.

    Bandeen-Roche et al. 2006 · J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med SciValidation in the Women's Health and Aging Studies cohorts
  20. 20
    9 yearsbefore frailty, exhaustion already separates people who become frail

    Exhaustion distinguished people who later became frail about nine years before onset, while slowness, low activity and weakness appeared about six years before. Each added frailty component was reached with a probability of about 0.4.

    Stenholm et al. 2019 · J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med SciTwo cohorts, 2,438 older adults followed 9 to 15 years (LASA and InCHIANTI)
  21. 21
    Weaker mitochondriain muscle predict faster loss of walking ability

    Among well-functioning adults aged 60 and older, slower muscle energy recovery after exercise, a measure of mitochondrial capacity, predicted greater decline in walking speed and 400-meter walk time over about 2.5 years. Loss of muscle strength and mass explained part of this link.

    Tian et al. 2022 · Aging CellCohort of 380 adults aged 60+ with muscle MR spectroscopy (Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging)
  22. 22
    Less energy, more immunityproteins in aging human muscle

    Muscle from older healthy people had fewer ribosome and energy metabolism proteins, including mitochondrial ones, and more proteins tied to immunity, protein quality control and RNA splicing, pointing to impaired energy production and a pro-inflammatory environment.

    Ubaida-Mohien et al. 2019 · ElifeProteomics of muscle biopsies from 58 healthy people aged 20 to 87
  23. 23
    12% fewer caloriesfor two years shifted muscle gene activity toward stress resistance and longevity pathways

    In healthy people randomized to eat about 12% fewer calories for two years, muscle showed changes in genes for protein quality control, DNA repair, mitochondrial growth, circadian rhythm and inflammation. Some of these changes helped explain why muscle quality was preserved despite a small loss of muscle mass.

    Das et al. 2023 · Aging CellRNA sequencing of muscle biopsies from 90 participants in the CALERIE randomized trial
  24. 24
    1 in 3cases of anemia in older Americans have no identifiable cause

    About 11% of men and 10% of women aged 65 and older in the US were anemic, rising past 20% at age 85 and older. A third of cases came from nutrient deficiencies, a third from chronic inflammation or kidney disease, and a third had no clear cause.

    Guralnik et al. 2004 · BloodNational survey of non-institutionalized US adults (NHANES III, 1988-1994)
  25. 25
    22% higherrisk of death for every 1% increase in red blood cell size variation

    Red blood cell distribution width, a routine part of a blood count, strongly predicted death in adults 45 and older. The top fifth had 2.1 times the risk of the bottom fifth, and the link held in people without anemia or vitamin and iron deficiencies.

    Patel et al. 2009 · Arch Intern MedNational cohort of 8,175 US adults aged 45+ (NHANES III) followed to 2000
  26. 26
    Earlier menopauselinked to faster epigenetic aging of blood

    Women with earlier menopause or removal of both ovaries had older-looking blood DNA methylation for their age. Genetic (Mendelian randomization) analysis suggested menopause itself speeds up epigenetic aging of blood.

    Levine et al. 2016 · Proc Natl Acad Sci U S AEpigenetic clock analysis in 4 studies, about 3,100 women
  27. 27
    1.55xhigher odds of physical decline with depressive symptoms

    Older people with depressed mood were 1.55 times as likely to decline on physical performance tests over four years, even after accounting for their health. The link held among people who reported no disability.

    Penninx et al. 1998 · JAMAProspective cohort of 1,286 adults aged 71+ followed for 4 years (Iowa)

About this page

This page gathers Luigi Ferrucci's published papers and preprints from PubMed and Europe PMC. The summary and key findings are written from those papers, and every finding cites exactly one of them.

"Most important" puts the findings with the widest relevance first. "Newest" sorts by the year of each finding's paper.

This site is for education and is not medical advice.
